blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define a merger and a takeover, explain why firms combine, and trace what a merger means for workers, customers and rival firms.

blocks.heading: Merger and takeover
blocks.text: A merger joins two firms into one combined firm by agreement: the owners of both decide together that a single firm serves them better, and two names become one. A takeover is different in form: one firm buys control of another, which usually keeps trading under new owners. A reader of business news can tell them apart by asking who wanted the deal - agreement between both points to a merger; a buyer and a target point to a takeover.

blocks.heading: Why firms combine, and who feels it
blocks.text: Firms combine for scale. A merged firm runs one booking office where the two firms ran two, buys its inputs in bigger quantities, and reaches further on a shared delivery fleet. Where the two firms were each other's closest rivals, combining also removes a seller from the market, and the pressure of rivalry on prices may weaken with it: where customers have few alternatives, the combined firm is likely to face less resistance to a higher price. The consequences land unevenly. Workers in duplicated jobs may face cutbacks: one booking office needs one manager, not two. Customers may pay more where the rival that held prices down is gone. Rival firms now compete against a bigger firm with lower average costs.

blocks.heading: Two bakeries become one in Otavi
blocks.text: Otavi had three bakeries. In 2025 the two larger ones merged: before, one supplied 3 100 loaves a week and the other 1 900; the merged bakery now supplies 5 200 loaves a week from a single building. Within a year the town's bread price had risen from N$10 to N$12 a loaf. The merged firm wanted higher prices - firms generally do - but the want is not the cause: what changed is that the town's closest pair of rivals became one seller, and the remaining bakery now carries whatever pressure exists to hold prices down. Two bicycle makers in Osaka that merged show the other side of the same coin: shared factory costs on one side, one fewer competing brand in the shops on the other.

blocks.heading: Horizontal, vertical and conglomerate mergers
blocks.text: Mergers are named by how the two firms' activities relate. A horizontal merger joins two firms in the same industry at the same stage of production: two bakeries, two banks, two bus companies - the Otavi bakeries above are an example. A vertical merger joins two firms at different stages of the same production chain. It is backward when a firm joins with its supplier, nearer the raw material - a bakery merging with the flour mill that supplies it - and forward when a firm joins with its customer, nearer the final buyer - the flour mill merging with a chain of bakeries, or a brewery with a chain of bars. A conglomerate merger joins firms in unrelated industries: a Walvis Bay fishing company merging with a Windhoek furniture maker. Large business groups in Japan and South Korea grew partly in this way, holding firms in shipbuilding, electronics and insurance under one owner.

blocks.heading: What each type of merger offers, and what it risks
blocks.text: A horizontal merger offers the clearest economies of scale - one office, one delivery fleet, bigger orders for inputs - and a larger market share. Its risks fall largely on others: customers may pay more where the merger removes a close rival, workers in duplicated jobs may lose them, and the larger firm may meet diseconomies of scale. A backward vertical merger secures the firm's inputs: the bakery that owns its mill can count on flour when flour is short, controls its quality, and no longer pays the miller's profit on top of the cost of milling. A forward vertical merger secures outlets: the mill that owns bakeries knows its flour has buyers, and it gains the profit the bakeries made. The vertical risks are that the firm loses the freedom to buy from a cheaper outside supplier, its managers must learn to run a different kind of business, and rival bakeries may find flour harder to obtain. A conglomerate merger spreads risk: a firm in two unrelated markets may keep earning when demand in one of them falls, as furniture sales may hold up in a poor fishing season. Its weakness is that the managers may know little about the new industry, and few production costs can be shared, so economies of scale tend to be small.
